title: 5 Ways To Be A Calmer, More Effective Teacher https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2012/03/10/5-ways-to-be-a-calmer-more-effective-teacher/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin connects teacher temperament directly to classroom behavior, arguing that a tense, uptight teacher produces a tense, unfocused classroom. He offers five practical techniques for cultivating calm: deciding in advance, before the school day begins, not to lose composure no matter what happens; physically slowing down movements and pace; speaking calmly during instructions while allowing passion during lessons; taking deep breaths regularly throughout the day; and mentally preparing by reviewing lesson plans and visualizing a calm, poised response to challenges. He closes by framing excitability as largely teacher-driven and fixable through this simple shift in mindset and habit, rather than an unavoidable feature of the job.
points: A teacher's own tension and stress translate directly into a more excitable, unfocused, and misbehavior-prone classroom.
Deciding, before the school day starts, not to lose composure regardless of what happens is presented as a simple but highly effective technique used by professional athletes.
Physically slowing one's pace and movements is said to calm the mind as well, improving observation and responsiveness.
Regular deep breathing throughout the day is offered as a fast, physiological way to reduce tension for both teacher and students.
Mental preparation — reviewing lesson plans and visualizing a poised response to challenges — helps produce physical calm before the day begins.
quotes: Because a tightly wound teacher translates to a tension-filled classroom—the kind of tension visitors can feel tingling in their sensory receptors the moment they enter your classroom.
Now decide that no matter what happens that day, no matter how crazy or how alarming, you will not lose your composure. And guess what? You won’t.
By slowing your movements to an easier-going, more graceful pace, your mind will slow down as well—becoming less distracted, more observant, and better able to respond to your students.
It’s remarkable what a few long, slow breaths can do. Almost immediately, blood pressure drops, your expression softens, and tension drains from your body.
Excitability in students is a major source of misbehavior, and in nearly every circumstance, teachers are to blame.
